View in browser                 Damian Paletta   Alaska Senate Bombshell Lays Bare the Shadowy Plots in Politics   Plus, the DOJ’s push against Trump’s rivals reaches a higher gear, and some Hispanic voters in Texas are turning on Republicans     NATHANIEL WILDER/BLOOMBERG NEWS   Good morning. It was always an eyebrow raiser. In late May, someone named Dan Sullivan filed paperwork in Alaska to try to unseat GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan.

   On Wednesday, an explosive article in the New York Times suggested this was no coincidence after all. The article alleges that the new Dan Sullivan was, in effect, recruited by staffers for Democratic candidate Mary Peltola as part of a campaign canvassing the state for people with this name (the Peltola campaign has denied any role in recruiting a spoiler).

   This so-called ballot-stacking tactic could tip the balance of Tuesday’s election. It will be very difficult to know how many voters are casting a ballot for Dan J. Sullivan Jr. (the new challenger) because they actually support him compared with how many are voting for him because they think he’s the actual senator (the ballot will identify Sen. Sullivan as a Republican and the incumbent, which might help avoid some confusion).

   Is all fair in love, war and politics? Not necessarily. The Justice Department has already filed a lawsuit over the matter, and Attorney General Todd Blanche last week (before the New York Times report) said it’s possible a crime was committed in Alaska. Trump on Wednesday said Peltola should “suffer the Legal and Political consequences” based on the New York Times story, though it doesn’t show that Peltola played a personal role in the recruitment effort.

   Trump called for Peltola to be removed from Tuesday’s ballot as punishment and said she should be prosecuted. Alaska’s Republican governor on Wednesday night also called for an investigation into the matter.

   Third-party candidates can shake up races. Look at Ross Perot in 1992 or Jill Stein in 2016. They didn’t confuse voters, but their names also weren’t nearly identical to the candidates’.

   It’s one thing to siphon off votes, but to confuse voters?

   This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       People and Policies I’m Watching   GDP: Third-quarter gross domestic product data will be released at 8:30 a.m. ET.

   Interest rates: The Federal Reserve held rates steady on Wednesday but two officials sought another increase.

   Trump’s Thursday: The president is scheduled to leave the White House early for Rock Hill, S.C., to hold a midterm rally at 12:30 p.m. Later he will host Halloween at the White House at 5:30 p.m. and he has a tele-rally starting at 7 p.m.

       What I’m Following     TIERNEY L. CROSS/PRESS POOL   The Justice Department’s push against Trump’s foes reaches a higher gear. With the midterms looming, the Justice Department has attempted a frenzy of legal maneuvers to advance President Trump’s demands to prosecute his political foes. The blitz comes as Justice Department leadership is under pressure to show progress before Election Day on Trump’s priorities, people familiar with the matter say.

   Some Hispanic voters are turning on Trump and putting Texas in play. As Texans head to the polls to decide some of the nation’s most closely watched races, Latino voters could once again play a decisive role . A recent Wall Street Journal poll found 53% of Latino voters picking a Democrat for Congress over a Republican, while 35% chose a Republican.

   Vance reaches out to Iranian hard-liner in bid to restart peace talks. Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei to revive peace negotiations even as President Trump threatens to restart the war after next week’s midterm elections, U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter said.

       What Else Is Happening   • These Gen Z men voted for Trump —some now wish they hadn’t.

   • The Trump administration’s stock portfolio spans more than 40 companies.

   • Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms is neck and neck with Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in the Georgia governor’s race .

   • Flávio Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Miami using decoys, a private jet and a friend in the White House.

   • The U.S. expelled a Cuban diplomat after an extraordinary verbal clash at the United Nations.

   • Tech giants are ramping up resistance to ICE in a bid to avoid Democratic scrutiny.

What I’m Following

 
 
TIERNEY L. CROSS/PRESS POOL
 

The Justice Department’s push against Trump’s foes reaches a higher gear. With the midterms looming, the Justice Department has attempted a frenzy of legal maneuvers to advance President Trump’s demands to prosecute his political foes.
